issues.legal_issue: Under Hindu law, lunacy existing when succession opens excludes an heir from inheritance even if the lunacy is not congenital.
material_facts: The person whose entitlement to inherit was disputed was found to be a lunatic when succession opened.
The asserted disability was lunacy, rather than idiocy, and the argument that it had to be congenital was rejected.
issues.conclusion: Lunacy, unlike idiocy, need not be congenital to exclude a person from inheritance; it is sufficient that the lunacy existed when succession opened.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed Manu IX.201 and considered the related texts of Narada XIII.21–22, Yajnavalkya II.140–141, Saraswati Vilasa 148 and Smriti Chandrika, chapter V, paragraph 4. It approved Muthusami v. Meenammal, Wooma Pershad Roy v. Grish Chunder Prochundo and Deo Kishen v. Budh Prakash, and disapproved the contrary observations in Murarji Gokuldas v. Parvatibai and Sanku v. Puttamma. It also noted that the Hindu Inheritance (Removal of Disabilities) Act XII of 1928 made madness from birth a ground of exclusion prospectively, consistent with the judicial interpretation of the earlier law.

rule.if: hindu_inheritance_dispute and lunacy_at_succession and condition_was_lunacy_not_idiocy and not congenital_disability

predicates.hindu_inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a person is entitled to inherit under Hindu law.
predicates.lunacy_at_succession: The person had lunacy when the succession opened.
predicates.condition_was_lunacy_not_idiocy: The relevant mental condition was lunacy rather than idiocy.
predicates.congenital_disability: The relevant disability existed from birth.
predicates.lunacy_excludes_from_inheritance: A person with lunacy when succession opens is excluded from inheritance.

issues.definition: When an inheritance dispute concerns a person whose lunacy existed at succession but was not congenital and was not idiocy, that lunacy excludes the person from inheritance.

issues.legal_issue: The evidence established that the person was a lunatic when succession opened.
material_facts: In litigation brought by several relatives over a period of years, the person was repeatedly treated as a lunatic requiring a guardian or next friend.
In a court inquiry, a court officer visited the person, who did not answer even a simple question about his name; the officer reported that the person appeared vacant and unable to answer.
The person’s relatives did not assert his claim to a share in an arrangement concerning the property, and the evidence as a whole supported the finding of lunacy.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the finding that the person was a lunatic when succession opened, rejecting the distinction between lunacy and mere weakness of intellect on the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the evidence as a whole, including the long and continuous conduct of relatives in treating the person as a lunatic and the contemporaneous court inquiry. It found that the preponderance of probabilities supported the High Court’s factual conclusion.

predicates.inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns a person's entitlement to inherit.
predicates.relatives_repeatedly_treated_person_as_l: Relatives repeatedly treated the person as a lunatic requiring representation in legal proceedings.
predicates.court_inquiry_found_inability_to_answer_: A court inquiry found that the person could not answer simple questions and appeared mentally incapacitated.
predicates.person_found_to_be_lunatic_at_succession: The person is found to have been a lunatic when succession opened.

issues.definition: In an inheritance dispute, repeated treatment as a lunatic by relatives together with a court inquiry showing inability to answer simple questions supports a finding that the person was a lunatic at succession.

issues.legal_issue: The alleged family arrangement giving the person a share was not proved.
material_facts: An affidavit filed in another proceeding said that several claimants agreed to give the person a share, but did not record that the arrangement had been completed.
The claimants said to have given the share were not examined as witnesses.
No application was made to transfer the relevant land records to reflect the alleged arrangement.
issues.conclusion: The person’s entitlement to a share on the basis of the alleged family arrangement was not established.
issues.legal_principle: A claimant relying on a family arrangement must establish that the arrangement was made; an affidavit that does not show a completed arrangement, unsupported by testimony from the alleged participants and by any application to reflect the arrangement in the land records, was insufficient on these facts.

rule.if: inheritance_share_claim and alleged_family_arrangement and affidavit_did_not_show_completed_arrangement and alleged_participants_not_examined and no_land_record_transfer_application

predicates.inheritance_share_claim: A person claims an inheritance share on the basis of an arrangement among family members.
predicates.alleged_family_arrangement: The claimant alleges that family members agreed to give the person a share.
predicates.affidavit_did_not_show_completed_arrange: The affidavit relied on as evidence described a proposed or intended arrangement rather than a completed arrangement.
predicates.alleged_participants_not_examined: The people said to have made the arrangement were not examined as witnesses.
predicates.no_land_record_transfer_application: No application was made to change the land records to reflect the alleged arrangement.
predicates.family_arrangement_not_proved: The alleged family arrangement is not established.

issues.definition: A claimed family arrangement is not proved where the supporting affidavit does not establish a completed arrangement, the alleged participants are not examined, and no application is made to reflect the arrangement in the land records.

issues.legal_issue: A possession claim concerning property covered by an unexecuted decree was not barred because the evidence supported a finding that possession had already been obtained otherwise than through execution.
material_facts: The claim concerned property covered by a decree that had not been executed.
The courts below found that possession had been obtained otherwise than by execution of the decree.
Evidence included an admission by a witness that the deceased was in possession of the suit properties and payment of taxes by an heir for the relevant years.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent finding that possession had been obtained otherwise than through execution and rejected the contention that the possession claim was barred.
issues.legal_principle: The appellant relied on section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but the Court held that the concurrent factual finding of possession otherwise than by execution was supported by evidence and gave no reason to interfere.

predicates.possession_claim_based_on_unexecuted_dec: The proceeding includes a claim to possession of property covered by a decree that was not executed.
predicates.concurrent_finding_of_possession_outside: The courts below found that possession had been obtained otherwise than by executing the decree.
predicates.evidence_supports_that_finding: Evidence, including testimony about possession and payment of taxes, supports the finding that possession had been obtained.
predicates.limitation_bar_rejected: The contention that the possession claim is barred is rejected.

issues.definition: Where a possession claim concerns property under an unexecuted decree and supported concurrent findings establish possession outside execution, the limitation objection is rejected.
